title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
summary: Defines the Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4), the inter-autonomous-system routing protocol of the Internet, together with its companion RFC 1772. It was a draft standard and has been replaced by RFC 4271.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is how separate networks, each run by its own organisation, tell one another which addresses they can reach. Each router advertises the address ranges it can reach along with a list of the networks the advertisement has crossed, so that routing loops can be spotted and refused. A router that receives several advertisements for the same address chooses between them using a set of rules the RFC lays out in full.

questions: what are the bgp message types
how does bgp prevent routing loops
subtitle: The original rulebook for how separate networks exchange reachability information.

tldr.problem: Networks run by different organisations have to tell each other which destinations they can reach, and each organisation has to keep its own routing decisions to itself rather than describe every internal path.
tldr.mechanism: BGP runs over TCP between speakers in different autonomous systems. Each speaker advertises IP prefixes together with path attributes, including the list of autonomous systems the route has crossed, and picks between the routes it receives using a degree of preference and a fixed set of tie-breaking rules.
tldr.outcome: The scheme lets each network keep its own interior routing while the network of networks shares reachability. The document was a Draft Standard and has been replaced by RFC 4271.

today: RFC 1771 was published in March 1995 as a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4271, which is the current specification of BGP-4. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1654.

sections.title: What BGP Is For
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol. Its primary function is to exchange network reachability information with other BGP systems, and that information includes the list of autonomous systems the reachability information traverses. That is enough to build a graph of how the systems connect, from which routing loops may be pruned and some policy decisions may be enforced at the level of the autonomous system.

An autonomous system is a set of routers under a single technical administration, using an interior gateway protocol and common metrics to route packets inside it and an exterior gateway protocol to route packets to other systems. The RFC stresses the point that an autonomous system may now use several interior protocols and several sets of metrics, but to the other systems it must present one coherent interior routing plan and a consistent picture of what is reachable through it.

The policy that BGP can enforce is a simple one: a BGP speaker advertises to its peers only those routes that it itself uses. This is the hop-by-hop routing paradigm, and BGP can enforce any policy that fits it, but it cannot make traffic take a different route than the traffic originating next door. BGP-4 adds support for classless interdomain routing: an IP prefix is advertised instead of a network class, the notion of class is dropped, and routes can be aggregated, including aggregation of AS paths, which is what makes the proposed supernetting scheme possible.

BGP runs over TCP, using TCP port 179, so the protocol does not need its own fragmentation, retransmission, acknowledgement or sequencing. Any authentication scheme used by the transport protocol may be used in addition to BGP's own.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP lets networks with different owners exchange information about which addresses they can reach. A network advertises only the routes it actually uses, so each side keeps its own internal decisions to itself. The advertisement also carries the list of networks the route has crossed, which is what makes loops detectable.

sections.title: Routes, Tables and the Life of a Session
sections.content:
Two systems form a transport protocol connection and exchange messages to open and confirm the connection parameters. The initial data flow is the entire BGP routing table; after that, incremental updates are sent as the tables change, and BGP does not require a periodic refresh. A speaker must therefore retain the current version of the whole routing table of every peer for the life of the connection. KeepAlive messages are sent often enough to keep the connection alive, and a Notification message is sent on an error, after which the connection closes.

A route is a unit of information that pairs a destination with the attributes of a path to that destination. Routes are advertised between peers in UPDATE messages and are stored in three routing information bases. The Adj-RIBs-In hold what peers have advertised, unprocessed. The Loc-RIB holds the routes the speaker has selected by applying its local policies to those. The Adj-RIBs-Out hold what it has selected for advertisement to peers. The RFC notes that the model does not require three separate copies to be kept; that is a local implementation choice.

A route is taken out of service in one of three ways: the prefix is listed in the WITHDRAWN ROUTES field of an UPDATE, a replacement route with the same reachability information is advertised, or the connection between the two speakers is closed, which implicitly removes every route they had advertised to each other.

Connections between speakers in different autonomous systems are external links, and connections between speakers inside one autonomous system are internal links. A connection between two speakers passes through a fixed sequence of states: Idle, in which incoming connections are refused, then Connect and Active, in which the transport connection is being set up, then OpenSent and OpenConfirm, in which the OPEN message is exchanged and confirmed, and finally Established, in which UPDATE, KEEPALIVE and NOTIFICATION messages flow. If both sides try to open a connection at the same time, one of the two is closed, and the rule is to keep the connection started by the speaker with the higher BGP Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: When a BGP session starts, one side sends its whole routing table and then sends changes as they happen. Each router keeps three tables: what peers told it, what it decided to use, and what it will pass on. A route is withdrawn by sending it back as a withdrawal, by replacing it, or by dropping the session.

sections.title: The Four Message Types
sections.content:
Every message has a fixed-size header of 19 octets, followed by data that depends on the type. The Marker is a 16-octet field the receiver can predict: it must be all ones for an OPEN message, or for an OPEN message that carries no authentication information, and otherwise it is computed by the authentication mechanism. It is used to detect loss of synchronisation between peers. The Length is a two-octet number giving the total length of the message including the header; it must be at least 19 and no greater than 4096, and no padding is allowed after the message. The Type is one octet: 1 for OPEN, 2 for UPDATE, 3 for NOTIFICATION and 4 for KEEPALIVE.

The OPEN message is the first message each side sends. It carries the protocol version, the sender's own autonomous system number, the hold time the sender proposes, its BGP Identifier, and optional parameters encoded as a type, length and value triplet. The hold time is the number of seconds that may elapse between successive KEEPALIVE or UPDATE messages; the value used is the smaller of the two sides' configured and proposed values, and it must be either zero or at least three seconds. The BGP Identifier is an IP address assigned to the speaker, fixed at startup and the same for every local interface and every peer. The minimum OPEN message is 29 octets.

An UPDATE message advertises a single feasible route and may withdraw several others at the same time. It has a two-octet Unfeasible Routes Length followed by the withdrawn prefixes, a two-octet Total Path Attribute Length followed by the path attributes, and the Network Layer Reachability Information holding the prefixes being advertised. The length of the reachability information is not written down; it is the message length minus 23 minus the two length fields. A prefix is written as a one-octet length in bits followed by the prefix itself, padded to an octet boundary. The minimum UPDATE message is 23 octets.

A KEEPALIVE message is the header alone, 19 octets long, and is sent often enough that the hold timer does not expire; a reasonable maximum gap is a third of the hold time, and they must not be sent more than once a second. If the negotiated hold time is zero, no periodic keepalives are sent. A NOTIFICATION message reports an error, after which the connection closes immediately; it carries an error code, an error subcode and diagnostic data, and its minimum length is 21 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every BGP message starts with the same 19-byte header: a marker to catch a desynchronised stream, a length, and a type number. There are four types: OPEN to start the session, UPDATE to send routes, KEEPALIVE to show the session is alive, and NOTIFICATION to report an error and close the connection.

sections.title: Path Attributes
sections.content:
Every UPDATE carries path attributes, each a triple of attribute type, attribute length and attribute value. The attribute type is two octets: an attribute flags octet followed by a type code octet. Four bits of the flags say whether the attribute is optional or well-known, whether it is transitive, whether the information it holds is partial, and whether the length field is one or two octets.

Attributes fall into four categories. Well-known mandatory attributes must be recognised by every implementation and must appear in every UPDATE. Well-known discretionary attributes must be recognised but may be left out. Optional transitive attributes may be unknown to a speaker, in which case the path is still accepted and the attribute is passed on with the partial bit set. Optional non-transitive attributes that are not recognised are quietly ignored and not passed on.

Seven attributes are defined. ORIGIN (type code 1) is well-known and mandatory; it says whether the reachability information is interior to the originating system (0), was learned through EGP (1), or was learned some other way (2). AS_PATH (2) is well-known and mandatory and lists the autonomous systems the information has crossed, as AS_SEQUENCE segments holding an ordered list and AS_SET segments holding an unordered one; a speaker that passes a route to a neighbouring system prepends its own AS number. NEXT_HOP (3) is well-known and mandatory and gives the IP address of the border router to use to reach the destinations in that UPDATE. MULTI_EXIT_DISC (4) is an optional non-transitive four-octet number used to pick between several exits into the same neighbouring system; it is never propagated to neighbouring systems. LOCAL_PREF (5) is well-known and discretionary and tells other speakers in the same autonomous system how much the originating speaker prefers this route; it is never sent to neighbouring systems and is ignored if received from one. ATOMIC_AGGREGATE (6) has length zero and tells other speakers that a less specific route was chosen without the more specific routes it covers. AGGREGATOR (7) is an optional transitive attribute of length six that records the last AS number to have formed an aggregated route and the IP address of the speaker that formed it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertised route carries a set of attributes. Three are mandatory: where the information came from, the list of networks it has crossed, and the address of the border router to send the traffic to. The rest are optional hints, such as how much a router prefers this path, and how a reader should treat an attribute it does not recognise.

sections.title: Choosing a Route and Avoiding Loops
sections.content:
The Decision Process applies local policy to the routes in the Adj-RIBs-In and produces the routes that will be advertised. It works in three phases. Phase 1 calculates a degree of preference for each route received from a neighbouring system; the function that computes it may not take the existence or non-existence of other routes, or the path attributes of other routes, as inputs, so that the result depends only on the route itself. Phase 2 chooses the best route for each destination and installs it in the Loc-RIB, looking up the immediate next hop in the interior routing protocol. Phase 3 disseminates the Loc-RIB to neighbouring peers according to local policy, optionally aggregating routes as it goes.

When several routes to the same destination have the same degree of preference, the tie is broken in a fixed order. First, if the system is configured to use MULTI_EXIT_DISC and the candidates differ in it, the route with the lowest value wins. Otherwise the route with the lowest interior cost to the next hop wins. If the costs are equal, a route advertised by a speaker in a neighbouring autonomous system is preferred, and if there are several of those, the one from the speaker with the lowest BGP Identifier wins; failing that, the route from the speaker with the lowest BGP Identifier wins.

One rule exists to prevent routing loops: if the local autonomous system appears in the AS path of a new route, that route cannot be better than any other route, because using it would send traffic back around. The RFC also notes that an autonomous system should avoid using unstable routes and should not make rapid spontaneous changes to its choice of route.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that hears several routes to the same address picks one by a fixed order: the router's own preference first, then the shortest internal path to the next hop, then a tie-break on identifiers. One rule overrides all of them: if the route's list of crossed networks already contains this network, the route is not used, because sending traffic along it would loop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit that security issues are not discussed in the document. The only authentication it defines is an optional Authentication Information parameter in the OPEN message, carrying a one-octet authentication code and variable authentication data, together with a rule for computing the Marker field from that mechanism. It also notes that a separate authentication mechanism may be used when establishing the transport connection, and that any scheme used by the transport protocol may be used in addition to BGP's own.

What the document does define is how a peer is checked for having the right identity in the first place. The OPEN message carries the sender's autonomous system number, and a peer that receives an unexpected value reports a Bad Peer AS error. It carries a BGP Identifier, which must be a valid IP address assigned to the speaker, and a mismatch is a Bad BGP Identifier error. Where two speakers open connections to each other at the same time, one connection is closed, and the rule compares the two BGP Identifiers as four-octet unsigned integers and keeps the one started by the higher value.
sections.plainLanguage: This version of BGP says little about security: authentication is an optional extra in the opening message. What it does insist on is that a peer prove which network it belongs to and that its identifier is a real address, and it gives a rule for settling the case where two routers connect to each other simultaneously.

fields.name: Marker
fields.desc: 16 octets. All ones for an OPEN message; otherwise computed by the authentication mechanism. Detects loss of synchronisation.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message including the header, from 19 to 4096 octets. No padding is allowed.

items.label: ORIGIN
items.desc: Well-known mandatory. 0 interior to the originating AS, 1 learned via EGP, 2 learned some other way.

items.label: AS_PATH
items.desc: Well-known mandatory. The autonomous systems the information has crossed, as AS_SET and AS_SEQUENCE segments.

items.label: NEXT_HOP
items.desc: Well-known mandatory. The IP address of the border router to use for the destinations in the UPDATE.

items.label: MULTI_EXIT_DISC
items.desc: Optional non-transitive. A metric used to choose between several exits into the same neighbouring AS.

items.label: LOCAL_PREF
items.desc: Well-known discretionary. The originating speaker's degree of preference, sent only inside the local AS.

items.label: ATOMIC_AGGREGATE
items.desc: Well-known discretionary, length zero. A less specific route was chosen without the more specific ones it covers.

items.label: AGGREGATOR
items.desc: Optional transitive, length 6. The last AS number and the speaker address that formed an aggregated route.
